BCG’s Asia-Pacific edition of its global AI at Work survey, covering more than 6,300 employees across nine markets, finds that AI adoption is widespread but value creation remains uneven. The decisive factor is not access to tools alone, but leaders’ clarity about AI’s purpose, roles, and expected outcomes.

Adoption is broad, but deep use remains limitedAPAC workers use AI slightly more than peers globally, yet only 26% use it frequently across most daily tasks. Those deeper users save over 14 hours weekly and are far likelier to report measurable impact.

Strategic clarity matters more than tool deploymentEmployees given strong AI direction report results even when tools are limited: 75% in APAC see positive impact. Clear priorities, roles, and instructions for reinvesting saved time unlock far more value than technology access alone.

Governance and training are lagging the pace of adoptionOnly 27% of APAC employees report adequate AI training, while fewer than four in ten have clear human-AI operating rules or ethical safeguards. Without these foundations, organizations cannot safely scale AI into core work.

Well-guided AI can make work harder—and more rewardingAI shifts employees from routine tasks toward judgment and oversight, increasing cognitive load for 47% of well-guided users. But 76% also enjoy work more, suggesting that purposeful redesign can outweigh anxiety.

More and more workers in Asia-Pacific use AI regularly. And it’s not just happening at the top, with 80% of frontline employees in APAC now using it at least several times a week, compared with 74% worldwide, a recent BCG survey shows.Yet not all companies are getting measurable value out of AI. The reason? Businesses are not providing the strategic clarity employees need: communicating AI as a strategic priority, clearly defining their AI strategy and employee roles, and giving meaningful guidance on what to do with the time they save. This clarity is a prerequisite for employees to move beyond deployment and begin reshaping their work from end to end and inventing new business models with AI. In fact, strategic clarity has more than five times the impact of simply providing AI tools, both in APAC and globally.Just 26% of APAC workers today say they use AI regularly and deeply (at least several times a week and in more than 50% of daily tasks). But these workers report an average time savings of more than 14 hours a week, while an impressive 69% report measurable impact from this effort. In contrast, those using AI on just a few tasks less than a few times a week report savings of only about 6 hours, and only 39% report impact.Simply deploying AI is clearly not enough; firms need to encourage employees to use AI frequently and across a wide variety of tasks. In addition, AI governance is essential. Just 27% of APAC workers today report sufficient AI training, while only 37% have received clear rules for human-AI teams and 39% are seeing ethical measures in place, significantly behind global numbers.This report takes a granular look at the use of AI and agentic AI in Asia-Pacific. These findings are revealed in this year’s APAC edition of our global AI at Work survey, conducted earlier this year. For the APAC edition, conducted in September and October, we queried more than 6,300 employees across nine APAC countries in a variety of industries about AI in the workplace. The results and our methodology are detailed in the accompanying slideshow.

APAC Is Still Marginally in the Lead
Looking back to our 2025 results, APAC held a significant lead in AI deployment, with 78% of workers using it versus 72% globally. Today, the numbers have nearly evened out, at 85% and 84%, respectively. Within these results, the most surprising finding is in Japan, where regular AI use at work has jumped from 51% of those surveyed to 79%—up 28 percentage points in just a year. Meanwhile, India—at a more developed stage—continues to lead the way in deployment, at 96%, while Korea trails our other survey regions, at 76%.Along with adoption, the time saved with AI varies widely as well, with India leading in hours saved per week, at 15, and Japan trailing at 6.8. In addition, 61% of workers in India and 60% in Australia say they put the time they save into accomplishing strategic tasks compared with just 32% to 35% in Thailand, Korea, and Singapore.Strategic Clarity Unlocks Value
Across APAC and globally, when strategic clarity is available to employees, the results are impressive. In fact, 81% of APAC workers who receive both strong clarity and strong AI tools from their firms report measurable impact, along with 83% worldwide. Meanwhile, 75% in APAC and 80% globally report positive impact from strong clarity even with limited tools. Further, employees who have clarity around what to do with the time they save are far more likely to invest that time into doing more strategic work (rather than doing other work or using the time saved as personal time), with 59% of those with strong clarity doing so, versus just 28% with no clarity.Nevertheless, strategic clarity around AI is falling short: just 20% of APAC employees have strong strategic clarity about AI. While 76% have received clear guidance on what to do with their saved time, only 39% have been given a clear AI strategy and understand their role, and 50% say AI has been communicated as a strategic priority.The “Joy Paradox”: Using AI Both Increases Cognitive Load and Boosts Enjoyment
AI allows workers to eliminate simple tasks from their day-to-day routine but adds the need for judgment and oversight, boosting the cognitive load as employee roles shift. Yet as APAC employees given real clarity and guidance increasingly use AI to reshape workflows or to invent new business models, their enjoyment of work increases along with their cognitive load, and anxiety remains relatively flat. This is the joy paradox. In fact, we find that 76% of APAC workers given strong strategic clarity are enjoying their work more since adopting AI, while 47% report a higher cognitive load. Yet only 7% report AI-related anxiety.

The next wave of value in APAC will come as firms make strategic clarity a top priority; focus on measurable impact rather than usage; encourage employees to use AI deeply, both across tasks and to reshape their work; and provide guidance and training—all while bearing in mind the extensive heterogeneity of the disparate regions within APAC and running a different playbook for every market.
